findings.short: Engineers worry that AI incident tools will deskill or replace them, and about what those tools can touch in production. On the pages checked, none of the {vendors_rated} options shows proof on either.
findings.headline: Deskilling or replacement, and production access: on the pages checked, every option asserts and none shows proof. Investigations and Rootly make the strictest promises on access.
findings.note: The model counts {count:deskills_or_replaces_engineers} deskilling or replacement posts and {count:data_access_and_security} on access. Claude then read each in full: {read:deskills_or_replaces_engineers:core} of the {count:deskills_or_replaces_engineers} are squarely about AI tools deskilling or replacing engineers, and {read:deskills_or_replaces_engineers:related} are related (skills lost to AI-written code, who is accountable, or the trade-off mentioned in passing). The rest don't fit. {read:data_access_and_security:core} of the {count:data_access_and_security} access posts fit squarely. The pipeline first rated Datadog's deskilling answer as shown; a review changed it to said, because a head start isn't evidence that engineers keep or build skills.
findings.implication: On deskilling, incident.io says engineers keep the final call, and that Nexus raises the floor for new hires. Nobody shows responders keeping their skills; Datadog comes closest, with one named customer saying newer engineers now begin with a head start, and another that it could raise skill levels. Showing what on-call engineers learn from its reasoning would be the first proof on this row of the map. On access, incident.io's product page says Investigations' only change is a pull request you review, as strict a promise as Rootly's sign-off on every change. Listing everything it can read, and showing how “pull request only” is enforced, would turn that promise into proof.
findings.why: Round 2 review (20 Oct), simulated: no ranking words (23 vs 20 is within label noise); counts given with a full read of both rows; credits incident.io's access promise and SOC 2; names Datadog as the nearest to proof on deskilling (engineer, competitive PMM and marketing-lead reviews). Round 3 review (20 Oct), simulated accuracy and decision panels: 'closest on access' was an opinion; 'only option to name an outside audit' rested on one page per competitor (their trust pages weren't checked); the read is regrouped more strictly; counts moved from the headline to the note. Daniyaal approved this as the lead (20 Oct). Round 4 review (21 Oct), simulated decision, competitive, engineer, editor and accuracy panels: the SOC 2 comparison rested on one page per competitor and doesn't answer 'what can it touch'; 'PagerDuty's and Resolve's agents act on their own' was a comparison for a private card, not a public page; only one Datadog customer mentions a head start; the pull-request promise is attributed to the product page; the note says Claude did the reading.
findings.title: No option answers two common worries with proof yet
findings.explain: Beyond whether the AI works, engineers worry about what it does to them and to their systems. The model counts {count:deskills_or_replaces_engineers} posts worrying that these tools will deskill or replace engineers, and {count:data_access_and_security} wary of giving an AI access to production systems or data. On the pages checked, every option makes claims on both, and none shows proof.

findings.headline: {diy:uses} of {n_base} posts use or recommend a general AI tool for incident work, {diy:uses:positive} of them positive about it; only {diy:uses:unneeded} of those {diy:uses} argue that makes a dedicated product unnecessary.
findings.implication: incident.io argues on its blog that in-house builds rarely measure accuracy, and ships a plugin for the agents engineers already use. It also tests Investigations daily on real past incidents, frozen so the agent sees only what responders had at the start. What's missing is a published score from those tests, and the same test run on a general agent with the same access. Showing the grading scale and how the incidents were chosen would let a sceptic judge the test as well as the score; a total needn't show any customer's data.
findings.why: Round 2 review (20 Oct), simulated: the 13 'product unnecessary' included 5 posts outside the 73 users; the subset is now computed (diy:uses:unneeded). Backtests can give a score without publishing customer incidents. Round 3 review (20 Oct), simulated accuracy and decision panels: the fair comparison is a general agent with the same access, not a bare model; an outsider shouldn't say what incident.io's data allows. Round 4 review (21 Oct), simulated decision, competitive, engineer, editor and accuracy panels: 'the comparison they reach for first' didn't follow from the data (only a minority make the comparison); backtests and frozen incidents explained in plain words; grading scale and incident choice added, the first things an engineer asks about a vendor's own benchmark.
findings.title: Many engineers already use a general AI tool for incident work
findings.explain: {diy:uses} of the {n_base} posts describe using or recommending a general AI tool, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor, for incident work, and {diy:uses:positive} of them are positive about it. Only {diy:uses:unneeded} of those {diy:uses} argue that this makes a dedicated product unnecessary. So it is less an objection than a habit, but it makes the tool they already use the likely yardstick for Investigations.

findings.headline: {either:wrong_or_hallucinated_cause+cant_verify_reasoning} of {n_base} posts say the AI gets the cause wrong or that its reasoning can't be checked.
findings.implication: The proof so far is a measured jump in accurate early updates, and an incident write-up in which its conclusion was checked against the code. Each customer can see its own accuracy on the Investigations homepage, and incident.io's buyer's guide tells evaluators to ask vendors for precision and recall. No option on the map publishes such a figure yet; one from its daily backtests would answer its own guide's question.
findings.why: Round 2 review (20 Oct), simulated: 'every hypothesis linked to its sources' is a feature claim, not proof; the cant-verify rating rests on the incident write-up. Round 4 review (21 Oct), simulated decision, competitive, engineer, editor and accuracy panels: 'where incident.io has done the most' was a judgement the map doesn't measure; fewer 'would be the first' endings. Round 4: the quote shown now asks for the error rate ("You need to quantify this. With actual numbers.", a reply to a founder saying it can be very reliable), which is what the title says; read in context by the accuracy reviewer.
findings.title: Engineers will ask how often it's wrong
findings.explain: {either:wrong_or_hallucinated_cause+cant_verify_reasoning} posts say the AI gets the cause wrong, or that its reasoning can't be checked. incident.io's pages show proof on both; on checking its reasoning, the only other option that does is one engineer's do-it-yourself write-up. The question sceptics ask next is how often it's wrong.
